summary: Describes common practice for how nodes should behave when originating and receiving RSVP-TE Path Error messages about a preempted MPLS or GMPLS traffic engineering label switched path. It documents existing behavior to improve interoperability. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network path gets bumped to make room for a more important one, the routers send out error notes. This document says what each router should do when it sends or receives one of those notes.

subtitle: What routers should do when they send or receive an RSVP-TE PathErr message about a preempted label switched path.

tldr.problem: When a traffic engineering label switched path (TE LSP) is preempted, nodes need to agree on what to do when they send or receive the resulting RSVP PathErr message, or implementations may behave differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC restates existing practice: a detecting node sends PathErr and, for fatal errors, clears Path and Resv state, while nodes that receive PathErr take no action on state.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new protocol extensions. It clarifies RFC 3209 so that non-conformant implementations are less likely, which the RFC says reduces security risk.

today: RFC 5711 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010 that updates RFC 3209. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This document describes common practice for a node that sends an RSVP-TE Path Error message, and for a node that receives one, when a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) or Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) traffic engineering label switched path (TE LSP) has been preempted. Preemption is defined in RFC 3209.

It covers only PathErr processing for that case. It does not define any new protocol extensions, and it updates RFC 3209 by clarification and restatement of procedures already set out there.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is a rule reminder for routers. It says what to do when a path is taken away to give room to a more important one.

sections.title: PathErr and Fatal Versus Non-Fatal Errors
sections.content:
RFC 2205 defines two RSVP error messages. PathErr messages travel upstream toward the head-end of the flow. ResvErr messages travel downstream toward the tail-end. PathErr messages are routed hop by hop using the path state set up when the Path message went from head-end to tail-end, and they do not modify the state of nodes they pass through.

The ERROR_SPEC object holds the address of the node that detected the error, an Error Code for the category and an Error Value that qualifies it. Values are kept in an IANA registry.

Errors are either fatal, meaning disruptive for the TE LSP, or non-fatal, meaning non-disruptive. PathErr can occur during LSP establishment or after the LSP is established.
sections.plainLanguage: An error note goes backwards along the path toward where it started. Some problems are big and stop everything, while others are small and the path keeps working.

sections.title: Behavior at the Detecting Node
sections.content:
For a fatal error, called Hard Preemption in Section 4.7.3 of RFC 3209, the detecting node MUST send a PathErr message and MUST clear the corresponding Path and Resv control-plane state. That also releases the data-plane resources, which disrupts traffic. The RFC notes that in fatal cases the LSP has usually already failed in the data plane. During establishment no traffic flows yet, so the effect differs from an active LSP.

For a non-fatal error, the detecting node should send a PathErr message and must not clear control-plane or data-plane state.
sections.plainLanguage: The router that has to bump a path tells everyone upstream, and then tears down its own record of that path. If the problem is only a warning, it sends the note but leaves everything running.

sections.title: Behavior at Receiving Nodes and the Data Plane
sections.content:
Every node upstream of the detecting node, including the head-end, receives the PathErr. Following RFC 2205, a receiving node takes no action on it and must not clear Path or Resv control-plane or data-plane state, whether the error is fatal or not. RSVP state should only change on a PathTear or ResvTear message, or when Path or Resv state times out.

RFC 3473 defines a Path_State_Removed flag in the ERROR_SPEC object. When set, it says the sender removed Path state and associated state. The receiver should do the same before forwarding, but may keep state and clear the flag before forwarding.

Any node that clears Path state, Resv state or both MUST also free the data-plane resources of that TE LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that only hear the note do not tear anything down on their own. They wait for a proper teardown message or for the record to time out, unless the note carries a special flag asking them to clean up too.

sections.title: Error Codes for a Preempted LSP
sections.content:
Two error codes report a preempted TE LSP, and both are fatal errors.

  • From RFC 2750: Error Code 2, "Policy Control Failure", with Error Value 5, "Flow was preempted".
  • From RFC 2205: Error Code 12, "Service preempted".
sections.plainLanguage: There are two official labels for the note that says a path was bumped. Both mean a serious problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines no new procedures. It clarifies procedures from other documents whose security considerations are already given in RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and it raises no specific security issues beyond those of existing MPLS-TE. By making the procedures clearer, it reduces the security risk introduced by non-conformant implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added, so nothing new can go wrong. Clearer rules also mean fewer routers doing the wrong thing by mistake.
